title: Going home
hook: John Muir: going to the mountains is going home
carry: nature's peace will flow into you

segments.voice: Yesterday, Emerson on a muddy common, and mean egotism, the self that vanished. Your line was nothing, seeing all. A new week starts today, in the mountains.

"Thousands of tired, nerve-shaken, over-civilized people are beginning to find out that going to the mountains is going home". John Muir wrote that in a book called Our National Parks. Tired. Nerve-shaken. Over-civilized. It reads like a crowded commute, or a long day of screens. When Muir watched worn-out city people heading for the hills, he didn't call it a getaway. He called it a homecoming.
screen: `TIRED, NERVE-SHAKEN, OVER-CIVILIZED.` → `HEADING FOR THE HILLS.` → `NOT A GETAWAY.`

segments.voice: Four turns in Muir's thought. First, the diagnosis. Over-civilized is a funny word, and a sharp one. In this sentence he doesn't attack towns; he names a tiredness that comes from too much indoors, too much noise, too little sky. Second, the reversal. Ordinary talk says the mountains are where you go away to. Muir flips it: the mountains are home, and the rest is the trip. Whatever people lose in the crowded streets, he suggests, they get back where the land is open. Third, wildness as need, not luxury. His sentence keeps going: "that wildness is a necessity; and that mountain parks and reservations are useful not only as fountains of timber and irrigating rivers, but as fountains of life." Timber and water are useful. Muir adds a third use you can't measure in boards or gallons: life itself. Fourth, what the mountains give. In the same book he writes: "Climb the mountains and get their good tidings. Nature's peace will flow into you as sunshine flows into trees." Good tidings is the King James Bible's phrase for good news, and some readers hear an echo of it here. For him the high country preaches, and its message isn't a doctrine. It's peace, freshness, and cares, he says, dropping off "like autumn leaves." Last week, poets and thinkers stood still and looked. Muir walks into the awe and calls it home.
screen: `TIRED AND OVER-CIVILIZED` · `GOING HOME, NOT AWAY` · `WILDNESS IS A NECESSITY` · `THE GOOD TIDINGS OF THE MOUNTAINS` · then, large: `GOING HOME.`

segments.voice: Let your eyes rest on the farthest thing you can see, a ridge, a rooftop line, a distant tree, the far end of a street; if there's none, close your eyes and remember a place in open country that felt like yours. Let your gaze go long and your shoulders drop. With each slow breath out, let one small care go, the way a leaf lets go of a branch.
Going home. John Muir's name for going to the mountains: not leaving real life behind, but coming back to it. Today's word.
Your line: nature's peace will flow into you. For Muir, the hills weren't the trip; they were home. That's day one thousand twenty-three.

howItsDone: Some people on a personal spiritual path treat time in wild country, a hike, a hill, a long view, as a regular practice of return, and Muir's writing is often read along the way.

chat.says: Why did John Muir call a trip to the mountains 'going home'?
options: He saw wildness as a need: tired people get back in the mountains what crowds take.
He grew up in the mountains, so a trip there meant visiting his childhood house.
He thought people should leave cities for good and live in the wilderness.
chat.meaning: Muir calls tired, over-civilized people's trips to the mountains going home: wildness is a necessity, and nature's peace flows into you like sunshine into trees.
